summary: Provides a problem statement and gap analysis for IP-based autonomic networking. It reviews what exists for self-management and where current network management depends too heavily on central control.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7576 asks what it would take for a network to manage itself in the way routing protocols already do. It looks at where networks already work this way, such as address assignment and time synchronisation, and at where people are still in charge, such as building the network, changing it and finding faults. It then lists the pieces that would have to be built, including a way for devices to try a change out before making it and a way for them to use what they have learned before.

questions: what is missing for self-managing networks
how do networks manage themselves today
subtitle: What a self-managing network would still be missing, and the mechanisms it would have to be built on.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols have always worked out their own state, but almost everything else in a network is configured from the top down by people working from templates, which is slow, error-prone and does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7576 reviews where autonomy already exists, lists the places where human judgement and central management still hold the network together, and names the missing general mechanisms: coordination between devices, reusable common components, a secure control plane, less configuration, a way to try changes out before making them, and a way to use what the network has already learned.
tldr.outcome: It is a gap analysis for a research group, not a specification. Its closing note is the important one: autonomic functions have to be secure from the start, because a network with weak autonomic functions is a network at risk.

today: RFC 7576 is an Informational RFC published in June 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is the gap analysis of an IRTF research group, written to point at the mechanisms that would have to exist before a network could manage itself.

sections.title: What Autonomic Networking Means Here
sections.content:
The goals and definitions for Autonomic Networking are set out in RFC 7575, and this document uses that terminology. The fundamental goal of an autonomic network is self-management, covering self-configuration, self-optimization, self-healing and self-protection. Interior gateway routing protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS largely show these properties already, while most other parts of networking require top-down configuration that often involves human administrators and a considerable degree of centralization.

In essence, Autonomic Networking puts all network configuration onto the same footing as routing, limiting manual or database-driven configuration to an essential minimum. The document is careful not to overstate this: it is highly unlikely to remove the need for human administrators, because many of their essential tasks will remain. The idea is to remove the tedious and error-prone tasks, such as manual calculations, cross-checking between two different configuration files, or tedious data entry. Higher-level operational tasks and complex troubleshooting will still be done by people.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to make the rest of the network work like routing does: the devices agree things out among themselves instead of being told what to do. That does not remove administrators. It removes the jobs that are tedious and easy to get wrong, such as calculating addresses by hand or checking that two configuration files agree.

sections.title: Where Autonomy Already Exists
sections.content:
For many years there was no alternative to completely manual and static management of IP addresses. Once a site had its address assignment, the subnet plan and the addressing plan were worked out on paper, prefixes were configured into routers by hand, and addresses were assigned to individual hosts by administrators, with the records kept in a text file or a spreadsheet. This was clumsy and error-prone as soon as a site had more than a few tens of hosts, but it had to be used until DHCP became viable in the second half of the 1990s. DHCP removed the need to configure hosts individually, though prefixes still had to be assigned to subnets and their routers by hand. Address management is tied to name management, because DNS records must be kept in step with address assignments, and reverse lookups meant that names had to be synthesised even for hosts that were only clients, so the DHCP tables and both kinds of DNS record had to be kept in step. Tools appeared to do that, but they are centralised solutions without autonomic properties. Prefix delegation in IPv6 is a related problem: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation is useful but needs specific configuration, and how to handle it in home networks is still being discussed.

Routing has been autonomic since the beginning. Making the network self-heal after a link or router failure was a goal from the start, and the problem of finding good routes was long ago a problem in graph theory with well known algorithms, so manual configuration of routing tables for a large network was never practical. Interior gateway routers still need some initial configuration to start, and BGP-4 routers need detailed static configuration of routing policy.

Other parts are largely in place. Configuring a default router in a host became automatic with DHCP for most IPv4 hosts, and in a simple home network the DHCP server sits in the same box as the router, so it is automatic there too; in more complex environments with a separate server or a relay, it is not. In IPv6 the default router comes from Router Advertisement messages from the router itself, which every IPv6 host uses, with no DHCPv6 involved, although open questions remain when more than one prefix is in use on a subnet and more than one first-hop router is available. Hostname lookup moved from a static hosts file to the DNS, and the addresses of the resolvers are now supplied automatically by DHCP or DHCPv6, or by a Router Advertisement option in IPv6, with Multicast DNS often used locally for extra automation of the name space.

User authentication and accounting moved from physical connectivity and the trust that follows from it to automated authentication with PPP and RADIUS in the early 1990s, where the accounting for a user starts automatically once the user authenticates. The authentication information itself is still managed by hand, and the picture gets complicated for mobile users who roam between operators, since prior relationships between the operators are needed. In security, many aspects depend on policy and central policy has to be applied strictly, but some mechanisms already show autonomic behaviour: IEEE 802.1x maps users into logical contexts after authenticating them, and BGP Flowspec allows a partially autonomic threat defence in which threats are identified and flow information is distributed automatically, with a person usually still checking the result. Negotiation capabilities in security protocols show simple autonomic behaviour, in that a policy about algorithm strength configured on servers propagates automatically to clients. State synchronisation between peers is another area: several devices start out with inconsistent state and go through a peer-to-peer procedure until their states agree, and network time synchronisation is a well-established explicit example of this.
sections.plainLanguage: Parts of the network already look after themselves. Routing has always worked out its own paths. Addresses are handed out by DHCP. IPv6 hosts learn their default router from the router itself. Hosts get their name server addresses the same way. Users authenticate themselves once and the accounting starts by itself. Time synchronisation is a good example of devices agreeing to a common state without anyone in charge.

sections.title: Where People Are Still in Charge
sections.content:
Building a network requires the operator to analyse the requirements, design the deployment architecture and topology, decide where equipment goes and how much capacity it has, set up the hardware, design the services, choose and enable the protocols, configure every device and every protocol, set up the user authentication and accounting policies and databases, and design and deploy the security mechanisms. These are complex jobs that cannot become fully autonomic in the foreseeable future, but parts of them might: the detailed device and protocol configuration, the population of the databases, and the initial management policies, which could be transplanted from another network and localised automatically.

Maintenance and management differ greatly between provider networks and enterprise networks. Provider networks change far more often, because they serve many customers with widely differing requirements, and the current rigid model is that administrators design a limited number of services for customers to order. A real-time request has to be met autonomically if the network is to be flexible and quick, but behind the interface, describing abstracted network information and managing user authorisation may depend on human intelligence for the foreseeable future. Identifying and consolidating users across networks or network services is another challenge, because many end users still manage their own accounts and authentication information by hand when they move between networks.

Classical maintenance mostly handles the configuration of devices, and remote management tools have made it easier, but each configuration detail is decided either by a person or by a rigid template, so those are the sources of all configuration errors: the human was wrong, the template was wrong, or both were. It is also a barrier to using resources well, because managers cannot respond quickly enough to events such as traffic bursts that the template did not foresee. That is why a light load is often assumed in network design, and why an overprovisioning ratio of at least 2 is normal. There is also concern that new, more flexible ways of configuring the network, of which Software-Defined Networking is the type, will only make the management problem more complex unless the details are managed automatically or autonomically.

Troubleshooting and recovery is where the current state is weakest. Network devices issue many warnings while running, but most are not precise enough to be identified as errors; some are early warnings that never become real errors, and others are effectively noise. During a major failure many devices issue multiple warnings in a short time, overloading the management system and the operators. For many scenarios human experience is still vital to identify real issues and locate them, though the situation could improve by automatically associating warnings from several devices together, and by learning from the historical relationship between warnings and actual faults. Some errors, particularly hardware failures, may always require a person. Autonomic management could still reduce the impact of errors, for example by switching traffic flows around, which today is manual apart from routing updates. Fixing software failures and configuration errors depends on people, and may involve rolling back a software version and rebooting hardware, which could be done autonomically if diagnostics and recovery functions were defined in advance. The document goes further and suggests predicting failures or overloads before they happen: a device could predict its own failure and warn its neighbours, or predict a neighbour's failure, and the network could then respond as if the failure had already occurred, by routing around the problem and reporting it, with no disturbance to users. The criteria for predicting failure could be temperature, battery status or bit error rates, and for predicting overload, increasing load factor, latency, jitter or congestion loss.
sections.plainLanguage: People still do the work that matters and that cannot be automated away: deciding what a new network should look like, deciding how customer services are shaped, and judging which warnings are real. But the document points at the parts that are held together by templates and habit. Networks are built assuming a light load because there is no way to react to a sudden flood, so twice the capacity is provisioned. Faults are fixed by hand, sometimes by rolling back software and rebooting. And it suggests devices could warn each other about an imminent failure, so the network could route around it before it happens.

sections.title: The Features an Autonomic Network Needs
sections.content:
There are innumerable properties of devices and end systems that today have to be configured by hand, by a script, or through a management protocol such as NETCONF. In an autonomic network all of these would need satisfactory default values or automatic configuration. Examples are parameters for tunnels of various kinds, flows, quality of service, service function chaining, energy management, system identification and time configuration. The task is to build up individual autonomic processes incrementally, so that they can later be combined to respond to every kind of network event.

The first missing feature is more coordination between devices or network partitions. Network services depend on a number of devices and parameters being in place in a certain order: after a power failure, a coordinated sequence of return-to-normal operations is desirable, with switches and routers first and name servers second. Today that sequence is known only to an administrator or written into a central script, and in a truly autonomic network the elements should understand their dependencies and resolve them locally. To make good decisions on their own, devices need more than reachability information from their neighbours, and they must be able to derive the dependencies between that information and their own configuration. Three kinds of interaction among peer devices are therefore needed: discovery, to find neighbours and peers; synchronization, to agree on network status; and negotiation, when something has to change. There is a need for reusable mechanisms of these three kinds, so that many types of device can be discovered, many types of parameter synchronized, and many types of objective negotiated.

The second is a set of reusable common components. Elements of autonomic functions already exist inside many protocols, but each has its own discovery, transport, messaging and security mechanisms and its own non-autonomic management interfaces, and it is often hard to extend an existing protocol to serve a different purpose. The reusable components should be able to identify other devices, users and processes securely; to secure operations automatically on the strength of that identity scheme; to manage any type of information and information flows; to discover peer devices and services for the various autonomic functions; to support closed-loop operations when a self-managing function involves more than one device; to be separable from the specific autonomic functions; and to be reusable by other autonomic functions.

The third is a secure control plane. The common components will in effect act as a control plane for autonomic operations, implemented in band as functions of the target network, in an overlay network, or out of band in a separate network. Autonomic operations can change how the network operates and allocate resources without human intervention or knowledge, so they must be secure. The control plane has to be designed to be secure against forged autonomic operations and man-in-the-middle attacks, and as secure as reasonably possible against denial of service attacks. It also has to be decided whether the control plane needs to resist unwanted monitoring, that is, whether encryption is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Three big pieces are missing. First, devices need to know what depends on what, so that they can bring a network back in the right order after a power cut without a script. That needs three reusable abilities between peers: finding each other, agreeing on the state of the network, and negotiating changes. Second, those abilities exist inside many protocols today, each in its own incompatible way, so they need to be pulled out into shared components. Third, because those components will change the network without asking anyone, the channel they use has to be secure against forged instructions and interception.

sections.title: Less Configuration, Dry Runs and Knowledge
sections.content:
Many existing protocols were defined to be as flexible as possible, so they need numerous initial configurations to start. There are choices and options that are irrelevant in any particular case, some targeting corner cases, and in protocols that have existed for years some design considerations no longer matter because the hardware has moved on. To appreciate the scale of this, more than 160 DHCP options have been defined for IPv4, and even sample router configuration files readily available online contain more than 200 lines of commands. There is therefore considerable scope for simplifying the operational tools for configuring common protocols, even if the underlying protocols cannot be simplified.

The deeper reason human decisions are often needed is a lack of information. When a device can collect enough information horizontally from other devices, it should be able to decide many parameters itself instead of receiving them from top-down configuration. It is desired that top-down management is reduced to the point where only the abstract intent is needed from administrators, and that neither users nor administrators need to create and maintain detailed policies and profiles; if they are needed, they should be built autonomically. The local parameters should be decided by distributed nodes themselves, from historic knowledge, analytics of current conditions, closed logical decision loops, or a combination of all.

Forecasting and dry runs are another gap. In a conventional network there is no mechanism for trying something out safely, so configuration changes have to be designed in the abstract and their probable effects estimated theoretically. Testing the changes on a complete and realistic simulator is impractical for a large network that is constantly changing, even with an accurate simulation, so applying changes to a running network carries a risk of failure. An autonomic network could close this gap by supporting a closed-loop dry run mode in which each configuration change is tested dynamically in the control plane without affecting the data plane. If the result is satisfactory the change is made live; if there is a consistency problem such as overcommitment of resources or incompatibility with another setting, the change is rolled back dynamically with no impact on traffic or users.

Finally, knowledge. The more knowledge and experience available, the better the decisions, and when one component lacks knowledge that affects what it should do while another has it, the knowledge is usually passed by an operator or a centralised tool. Up to now the only network knowledge available has been the current status inside a given device or the current status of other devices. Historic knowledge is very helpful in making correct decisions, in particular to reduce oscillation or to manage resources over time, and knowledge transplanted from other networks can help set up a new network or new devices. Knowledge of the relationships between network events and network configuration may help a network choose the best parameters from real performance feedback. Analytics of current conditions is another valuable source that autonomic nodes could use directly.
sections.plainLanguage: Two complaints run through this. There are too many settings to fill in: more than 160 DHCP options have been defined for IPv4, and a sample router configuration file runs to more than 200 lines of commands. And there is no safe way to try a change out, so changes have to be designed on paper and their effects guessed. The document asks for a dry run mode in which a change is tested in the control plane and can be rolled back if it does not fit, and for devices to use what the network has already learned instead of what a person tells them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document is about what is missing to allow autonomic network configuration, including security settings, so it does not itself create any new security issues. It is worth underlining, however, that autonomic technology must be designed with strong security properties from the start, since a network with vulnerable autonomic functions would be at great risk.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no security rules of its own, because it defines no new mechanism. Its warning is the important part: a self-managing network that can be fooled is more dangerous than one that waits for instructions, so the security has to be built in from the beginning rather than added later.

viz.caption: PARTS OF THE NETWORK THAT ALREADY LOOK AFTER THEMSELVES

items.title: Routing
items.text: Self-healing and path selection have been automatic since the protocols were designed.

items.title: Host addresses
items.text: DHCP hands out addresses and the details that go with them.

items.title: The default router
items.text: Supplied by DHCP for IPv4 and by Router Advertisement for IPv6.

items.title: The name server address
items.text: Also supplied by DHCP, DHCPv6 or a Router Advertisement option.

items.title: User accounting
items.text: Starts by itself once the user has authenticated with RADIUS.

items.title: Time synchronisation
items.text: Devices agree a common clock without anyone in charge.

viz.caption: WHAT THE REUSABLE COMMON COMPONENTS SHOULD BE ABLE TO DO

items.title: Identify securely
items.text: Recognise other devices, users and processes with confidence.

items.title: Secure operations
items.text: Protect actions automatically, using that identity.

items.title: Handle any information
items.text: Carry any type of information and information flow.

items.title: Find peers
items.text: Discover the peer devices and services that exist.

items.title: Close the loop
items.text: Support operations that involve more than one device.

items.title: Stay separate
items.text: Be separable from the particular function that uses them.

items.title: Be reused
items.text: Serve other autonomic functions as well.

viz.caption: THE JOBS PEOPLE DO, AND WHAT THE DOCUMENT SAYS COULD CHANGE

cells: People design it, place the equipment and configure every device
Part of it could be automatic, and initial policies transplanted from another network
A limited set of services designed by administrators, and templates for each setting
Real-time requests answered autonomously, and configuration that adapts to conditions
Detailed human work, or defaults that are too strict or too risky
Nodes identify each other, negotiate settings and find trust anchors by service discovery
Warnings are noisy, and software faults need a person to roll back and reboot
Warnings correlated across devices, faults predicted, and recovery functions defined in advance
